chapters.title: Chapter 5: Recent Shocks and the Investor's Playbook

lessons.title: 2020 to 2023: Stimulus, Inflation, and the SVB and Credit Suisse Failures

body.text: The medicine for one crisis can plant the seed of the next. Near-zero rates rescued the world in 2020, fuelled inflation by 2022, and the rate hikes that followed blew holes in the balance sheets of banks that had assumed rates would stay low.

children.text: On 8 March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank, the go-to bank for American tech start-ups, announced it had sold $21 billion of securities at a loss and needed to raise fresh capital. The next day, depositors pulled $42 billion. By the morning of 10 March, another $100 billion was expected to leave. Regulators shut the bank before it could open for business that day. SVB had not made reckless loans. It had bought safe US government bonds, just at the wrong interest rate.

Nine days later, Credit Suisse, a 167-year-old pillar of Swiss banking, was taken over by UBS in a weekend rescue. This lesson connects the pandemic stimulus of 2020 to the inflation of 2022 and the bank failures of 2023.

children.text: Build-up: The 2020 Rescue

When COVID-19 shut economies down in March 2020, central banks moved faster and further than in 2008. On 15 March 2020, the US Federal Reserve cut its policy rate to a range of 0% to 0.25% and announced $700 billion of bond purchases. On 23 March, it promised to buy bonds in whatever amounts were needed.

India acted too. The RBI allowed banks to offer a moratorium on loan instalments from March 2020, later extended to 31 August 2020, and on 22 May 2020 it cut the repo rate by 40 basis points to 4%, then a record low.

body.text: The 2020 response worked. Markets recovered and a financial crisis on top of the health crisis was avoided. But it also left banks holding huge deposits, which they invested in bonds paying very low interest. That quiet decision is where the 2023 story begins.

children.text: Trigger: Inflation and the Fastest Hikes in Decades

Supply chains broke, energy and food prices jumped after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and stimulus-fuelled demand came roaring back. US consumer inflation hit 9.1% in June 2022. India's retail inflation hit 7.79% in April 2022, an eight-year high and well above the RBI's tolerance band.

Central banks reversed course sharply. On 4 May 2022, the RBI raised the repo rate by 40 basis points at an unscheduled meeting, and kept going until it reached 6.5% in February 2023. The Fed raised its target range all the way to 5.25% to 5.5% by July 2023.

body.title: From emergency lows to inflation fighting: policy rates, 2020 to 2023

children.text: Why Rate Hikes Hurt Banks: Duration Risk
When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, because new bonds pay more. The longer a bond has left to run, the bigger the fall. The measure of that sensitivity is
duration

markDefs.definition: A measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to changes in interest rates. A bond with a duration of 6 loses roughly 6% of its value for every 1 percentage point rise in interest rates.

body.latex: \text{Change in bond price (\%)} \approx -\text{Duration} \times \text{Change in interest rate (percentage points)}
body.caption: A simple approximation that works well for moderate rate changes.

children.text: SVB had placed a large share of its deposits in long-term bonds, much of it classified as
held to maturity
. On paper, the losses did not count as long as the bank never sold. But if depositors withdrew money, the bank would be forced to sell, and the hidden losses would become real.

markDefs.definition: An accounting category for bonds a bank intends to keep until they mature. Their losses from rising rates are not recorded in reported profits or capital unless the bank sells them, so large losses can build up out of sight.

body.title: The Hidden Hole
body.prompt: A bank holds $60 billion of bonds with a duration of 6. Interest rates rise by 3 percentage points. Using the approximation above, how much value, in $ billion, have the bonds lost?
body.explanation: Price change ≈ -6 × 3 = -18%. Loss = $60 billion × 18% = $10.8 billion. If the bank has, say, $8 billion of capital, that unrealised loss is larger than all of it. As long as depositors stay, the loss can sit quietly in the held-to-maturity book. If they run, the bank must sell and the hole becomes real, exactly what happened to SVB.

children.text: Panic: The Fastest Bank Run in History

Chapter 2 showed deposit insurance ending bank runs in the 1930s. SVB shows why that protection has limits. About 89% of SVB's $172 billion in deposits was above the US insurance limit of $250,000, because its customers were start-ups and venture capital funds holding millions each. Those depositors were closely connected, watched the same news and could move money from a phone app in minutes.

body.title: Why So Fast?
body.question: SVB lost $42 billion in deposits in one day, far faster than bank runs in the 1930s or at Northern Rock in 2007. Which combination best explains the speed?
options: SVB had made large loans to risky borrowers, and the losses became public
Most deposits were uninsured and held by a tightly connected group of start-ups and investors who could withdraw instantly through digital banking
The US government announced it would not protect any SVB deposits
SVB was located outside the United States and not covered by US rules
body.explanation: Around 89% of SVB's deposits were above the insurance limit, so depositors had every reason to leave first. Its customers were concentrated in one industry, talked to each other constantly and followed the same investors, so fear spread in hours. Online and mobile banking let them move money in minutes, with no queue outside a branch. SVB's problem was not bad loans but losses on safe bonds, combined with a deposit base that could vanish overnight.

children.text: Credit Suisse: A Different Kind of Weakness

Credit Suisse was a global systemically important bank, not a regional lender. Its problems had built up for years through scandals, heavy losses and repeated restructurings, and clients had been withdrawing money for months. When SVB failed, confidence in weak banks everywhere collapsed, and Credit Suisse was the weakest of the large ones.
The rescue made history for a group of investors. Credit Suisse had issued
AT1 bonds

. As part of the UBS takeover, Swiss regulator FINMA ordered all of them, about CHF 16.5 billion, written down to zero, while shareholders still received some value in the deal. That ordering shocked bond markets, and in October 2025 a Swiss court ruled that the regulator's order lacked a sufficient legal basis, though the legal battle continued.

markDefs.definition: Additional Tier 1 bonds: a type of bank bond that counts as capital and is designed to absorb losses. If a bank gets into serious trouble, AT1 bonds can be converted into shares or written off completely, before depositors lose money.

body.title: Name the Bond
body.textWithBlank: The Credit Suisse bonds written off in March 2023 were Additional Tier ___ bonds, designed to absorb losses before depositors.
body.explanation: Additional Tier 1, or AT1. These bonds count as bank capital precisely because they can be written off in a crisis, which is why they pay higher interest than ordinary bank bonds.

children.text: The Indian Parallel: Yes Bank's AT1 Bonds

Indian investors had already learnt the AT1 lesson three years earlier. When Yes Bank was rescued in March 2020, a crisis you met in Chapter 1, about ₹8,415 crore of its AT1 bonds were written off completely on 14 March 2020. Many of the holders were individual investors who had been sold the bonds as safe, high-yield products.

body.label: Still in Court Years Later
body.value: ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank AT1 bonds written off
body.context: In January 2023, the Bombay High Court quashed the write-off, finding the reconstruction scheme had not explicitly authorised it. Yes Bank and the RBI appealed, and the Supreme Court stayed that order. The Supreme Court has reserved its verdict, and the matter remains before it.

children.text: India also moved on the SVB lesson. RBI rules for how banks classify and value their bond investments, effective 1 April 2024, tightened the use of the held-to-maturity category. Sales from it are capped at 5% of its opening value in a year without RBI approval, and banks cannot freely shift bonds between categories.

body.title: Go deeper: why the 2023 rescues looked different from 2008

children.text: After 2008, regulators promised that failing banks would no longer be rescued at taxpayers' expense. The 2023 failures tested that promise.

cells: SVB and Signature shareholders were wiped out; Credit Suisse shareholders received a small amount
At SVB and Signature, yes, through a special exception
AT1-style bonds were rare and mostly protected

children.text: The shift was partial. Bondholders at Credit Suisse took losses, a bail-in like Cyprus in Chapter 4. But US authorities still chose to protect all depositors at SVB and Signature to stop the panic spreading, showing that in a real run, containing contagion usually wins over strict rules.

body.title: The 9% Bank Bond
body.scenario: A relationship manager offers you a perpetual AT1 bond issued by a mid-sized Indian private bank, paying 9% a year, far more than the bank's fixed deposits. "It is issued by a bank regulated by the RBI, so it is basically as safe as a deposit," they say.
body.prompt: Using what happened at Yes Bank and Credit Suisse, explain what this bond really is, how it differs from a fixed deposit, and what you would check before buying.
body.modelAnswer: What it is: an AT1 bond is bank capital, not a deposit. It pays more precisely because it is designed to absorb losses if the bank gets into trouble. It can be written down or converted into shares before depositors lose money, and interest payments can be skipped. Perpetual means it has no fixed maturity; the bank may call it back on set dates but does not have to. How it differs from a fixed deposit: a fixed deposit is covered by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank and ranks above AT1 holders. An AT1 bond has no deposit insurance at all, and holders at Yes Bank in 2020 and Credit Suisse in 2023 lost their entire investment while depositors were protected. The claim that it is as safe as a deposit is wrong. What to check: the bank's capital ratios and how close it is to the trigger level that would allow a write-down; its asset quality, including gross and net NPAs; its deposit base and how concentrated or uninsured it is; the bond's exact terms on write-down, conversion and skipped interest; the call dates and what happens if the bank does not call; and whether SEBI and RBI rules on selling such bonds to individual investors are being followed. For most retail investors, a 9% yield is poor compensation for the risk of losing everything, and AT1 bonds should be treated as a high-risk product, not a deposit substitute.

cards.definition: How sensitive a bond's price is to interest rates. Duration 6 means roughly a 6% fall for each 1 percentage point rise.
An accounting category where losses from rising rates stay out of reported capital unless the bonds are sold.
Deposits above the insurance limit, $250,000 in the US and ₹5 lakh in India. They are the first to run.
Loss-absorbing bank bonds that count as capital and can be written off in a crisis, as at Yes Bank and Credit Suisse.
The Fed's March 2023 emergency loans to banks against government bonds valued at full face value.
A rate increase announced between scheduled policy meetings, like the RBI's 40 basis point hike on 4 May 2022.

points: The 2020 response of near-zero rates, huge bond buying and loan moratoriums prevented a financial crisis but helped fuel inflation
Inflation hit 9.1% in the US in June 2022 and 7.79% in India in April 2022, forcing the Fed to 5.25% to 5.5% and the RBI to a 6.5% repo rate
Rising rates created large hidden losses on banks' bond holdings; SVB's concentrated, 89% uninsured deposit base turned that into a $42 billion one-day run
Credit Suisse fell after years of weakness, and about CHF 16.5 billion of its AT1 bonds were written off in the UBS takeover, echoing Yes Bank's ₹8,415 crore AT1 write-off in 2020
India responded by tightening how banks classify and value bond investments from April 2024, and the core lesson for investors is that AT1 bonds and uninsured balances are not deposits

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The bond portfolio exercise and the AT1 scenario are hypothetical, and no bank or bond is being recommended or criticised. Legal proceedings on the Yes Bank and Credit Suisse AT1 write-offs were ongoing at the time of writing. Figures are drawn from Federal Reserve, FDIC, RBI, FINMA and other public sources.
